title: Static and Current Electricity
seo_title: Grade 9 Science (SNC1W): Static and Current Electricity Worksheets (Ontario)
standard_text: How charges behave in static and current electricity and how this relates to atomic structure; conductors and insulators; the components of a DC circuit with their symbols, quantities and SI units; and the difference between electricity and electrical energy. (summary of The Ontario Curriculum, Science, Grade 9: SNC1W (2022), Strand D: Principles and Applications of Electricity)
meta_desc: Free Grade 9 Science (SNC1W) worksheets on electricity: static charge, charging by friction and induction, conductors and insulators, circuit symbols, current, potential difference and electrical energy. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Only electrons move when objects are charged.
key_sub: Current I in amperes (A), potential difference V in volts (V), resistance R in ohms (Ω).
body_html:
How to think about it

Objects become charged by gaining or losing electrons: rubbing a balloon on hair moves electrons onto the balloon, so the balloon becomes negative and the hair positive. Like charges repel; unlike charges attract; a charged object also attracts a neutral one by induction.

In a conductor (metals) electrons move freely; in an insulator (plastic, rubber, glass) they do not. A circuit needs a source (cell or battery), a load (such as a lamp), conducting wires and a closed path. Current is measured with an ammeter in series; potential difference with a voltmeter in parallel. Electrical energy (in joules or kilowatt-hours) is what the current transfers to the load.

Example

A balloon rubbed on wool becomes negative. What happened?

Electrons moved from the wool to the balloon.

Answer: the balloon gained electrons

Example

How do you connect a voltmeter?

It compares two points.

Answer: in parallel across the component

Common mistakes

  • Saying protons move when objects become charged.
  • Connecting an ammeter in parallel.
  • Calling electricity and electrical energy the same thing.

items.q: Is polyethylene an electrical conductor or an insulator?
c: neither: it can never be charged
items.e: Conductors have charges (such as free electrons) that can move; insulators hold charges in place, so they can be charged by rubbing.

items.q: In a demo, two balloons carry charges that are negative and positive. What happens?
items.e: Like charges repel; unlike charges attract.

items.q: A perspex rod is rubbed with a woollen cloth and becomes positively charged. What charge does the woollen cloth gain?
items.e: Charge is transferred, not created: the two objects get equal and opposite charges.

items.q: A glass rod is rubbed with a silk cloth and becomes positively charged. Why?
c: Positive charges are made by friction.
Electrons move from the rod to the silk.
Protons move from the rod to the cloth.
items.e: Only electrons move when objects are rubbed; protons stay in the nuclei.

items.q: Clothes stick together after a dryer cycle. Which explanation is best?
c: The can's electrons are pushed to the far side, so the near side is positive.
Tumbling transfers electrons, so clothes get opposite charges.
Electrons moved from the hair to the balloon.
Protons moved from one object to the other.
items.e: Only electrons move between objects.

items.q: A negatively charged rod is held near a neutral metal sphere on an insulating stand. What happens to the electrons in the sphere?

items.e: In charging by induction, a nearby charged object pushes or pulls electrons; grounding lets electrons flow; the sphere ends with the opposite charge to the rod.
